| [THEORY-078](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-078.md) v2 | The top C eigenvalues of a trained C-class classifier's Fisher are carried by the second moment of its class-mean logit derivatives, so a cut at the bulk edge keeps the span of the class means, and they stand clear of the bulk to the extent between-class separation exceeds within-class variation | Papyan (2019), [LIT-619](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-619.md): for softmax cross-entropy the Gauss–Newton matrix G, which is the model's Fisher averaged over inputs, is an uncentred second moment of logit derivatives indexed by class and logit. It decomposes exactly into four terms (Eq. 28), and its top C eigenvalues match those of the class-mean term G₁. Papyan (2020), [LIT-613](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-613.md), splits those C into one global-mean outlier and C − 1 between-class ones, finds a C(C − 1) cross-class mini-bulk beneath them, and proves the whole pattern for a Gaussian toy model. Papyan (2018), [LIT-617](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-617.md), supplies the measurements and the attribution of the Hessian's outliers to G. The decomposition is algebra. That G₁ carries the outliers is measured, by eye, under a training protocol narrower than practice. So this is Proposed. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-080](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-080.md) v3 | In a linearised network with a Gaussian prior on its parameters, the Occam factor is a sum over the NTK's eigenvalues, so on spherical data each harmonic pays ½ log(1 + βnµ_k/α) and the kernel's eigenvalue decay schedules the complexity penalty across frequencies | The filer's synthesis, stated by no source. Its exact half is filed as the record's own claim, CLAIM-384; what stays here is the spherical account. A network linearised at initialisation, with an isotropic Gaussian prior on its parameters and Gaussian noise, is MacKay's linear-in-parameters model ([LIT-623](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-623.md)). Its Occam factor is −½ Σ log(1 + βλ_a/α) over the eigenvalues of JᵀJ. These are the empirical NTK's, which on uniform spherical data form Bietti & Bach's degree blocks, nµ_k with multiplicity N(d, k) ([LIT-608](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-608.md)). Degrees whose βnµ_k exceeds α pay about ½ log n per harmonic, and degrees below pay almost nothing. With µ_k ~ k^(−d), the number of paid directions γ grows as n^((d−1)/d), not as the parameter count. Basri et al.'s bound ([LIT-612](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-612.md), Eq. 14) is the matching data-fit term. The kernel's decay exponent is the schedule of the penalty. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-082](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-082.md) | Steepest descent is defined only relative to a metric, and Amari's proof that natural-gradient learning is Fisher efficient needs the Fisher information at the optimum to be invertible, the condition whose failure WBIC calls singular; in a multilayer perceptron it fails wherever an output weight is zero | Amari (1998), [LIT-607](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-607.md). Theorem 1 is a Lagrangian derivation: under \|dw\|² = Σg_ij dw_i dw_j the steepest-descent direction is −G⁻¹∇L, so it changes with G. Theorem 2 shows that online learning with step 1/t along the Fisher natural gradient attains the Cramér–Rao bound G⁻¹/t, and its proof uses G(w*)⁻¹. Watanabe, [LIT-616](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-616.md), Eq. 14, calls a truth regular when the optimum is one point and its Fisher is positive definite, and singular otherwise. From Amari's own Eq. 6.12, the score for hidden unit i's input weights carries the factor v_i. So the Fisher of a multilayer perceptron loses rank wherever an output weight is zero. That set is part of the optimum whenever the teacher needs fewer hidden units than the student has. Active because each step is checkable in the two texts. The claim that the Fisher is the only invariant metric is Chentsov's, cited and not held. | Active |
| [THEORY-083](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-083.md) | Training a classifier past zero training error collapses its last-layer features onto their class means and drives the centred means toward a simplex equiangular tight frame, with the classifier aligned to them and the decision becoming nearest class mean | Papyan, Han & Donoho (2020), [LIT-618](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-618.md), measured 480 trained classifiers on seven datasets with VGG, ResNet and DenseNet. Through the terminal phase, within-class variability of last-layer features falls (NC1), and the centred class means become equinorm and equiangular with cosine −1/(C − 1) (NC2). The classifier aligns with them (NC3), and the decision becomes nearest class mean (NC4). They prove that NC1 and NC2 imply NC3 and NC4 for the MSE-optimal and max-margin classifiers, and that the simplex ETF is the unique error-exponent-optimal codebook. Papyan (2020), [LIT-613](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-613.md), sees class means separate and grow more orthogonal with depth. The measurements cover one protocol, and the dynamics are unexplained outside free-features models. Within them, THEORY-278 (LIT-974) derives collapse for MSE under a re-whitened flow, and THEORY-286 (LIT-994) gives the cross-entropy endpoint under class imbalance. The paper's further claim, that the Hessian's class outliers are a symptom of collapse, is argued and not measured, and is left to [THEORY-078](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-078.md). | Proposed |
| [THEORY-084](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-084.md) v3 | Because the Gauss–Newton Fisher JᵀJ and the NTK Gram matrix JJᵀ share their non-zero spectrum, the lazy-regime Fisher of a ReLU network on spherical data inherits the NTK's harmonic-degree blocks, and a spectral threshold on it is well posed only at gaps between blocks | The filer's synthesis, stated by no source. The identity is linear algebra: JᵀJ (parameters × parameters) and JJᵀ (samples × samples) have the same non-zero eigenvalues. Under squared loss JᵀJ is the Gauss–Newton matrix and the Fisher. JJᵀ is the empirical NTK Gram matrix, which in the kernel regime on uniform spherical data has the degree-block spectrum of Bietti & Bach (2021), [LIT-608](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-608.md): µ_k with multiplicity N(d, k). The threshold claim draws on Cao et al. (2019), [LIT-624](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-624.md). Their guarantees are stated only for whole eigenspaces, with sample costs that grow as the gap below them shrinks. It also draws on Basri et al. (2019), [LIT-612](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-612.md), where a structural zero block shows up in a finite sample as small non-zero eigenvalues. No paper filed computes a Fisher spectrum in this regime. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-085](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-085.md) | A classifier's class-driven Fisher outliers pair each class's feature mean with that class's own error mean, so K-FAC's single Kronecker product of class-averaged factors adds every cross-class pairing and misplaces them, and differs from the class-wise product by the between-class covariance of its two factors | Papyan (2020), [LIT-613](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-613.md): per layer, the Fisher is a weighted sum of Kronecker products of features and backpropagated errors (Eq. 7.5), and its class outliers come from class means of gradients that are approximately h_c ⊗ δ_c. K-FAC (Martens & Grosse 2015, [LIT-622](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-622.md)) multiplies the class-averaged feature covariance by the class-averaged error covariance. Papyan finds its outliers and mini-bulks "drastically misaligned", and the class-wise CFAC aligns much better at deep layers. The filer adds a line of algebra: CFAC − K-FAC = Ave_c (H_c − H̄) ⊗ (Δ_c − Δ̄), so the two coincide when one factor's per-class statistics do not vary with class. The evidence is one MLP, spectra only, judged by eye. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-086](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-086.md) | In the kernel regime gradient descent fits the target eigenspace by eigenspace of the neural tangent kernel, at rates set by their eigenvalues; on uniform spherical data the eigenspaces are the harmonic degrees, and for fully connected ReLU networks the non-zero eigenvalues decay as k^(−d) at every depth | Three derived results that compose. Cao et al. (2019), [LIT-624](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-624.md), Theorem 4.2: for a wide two-layer ReLU network, the training residual's component in the top-r_k NTK eigenspace falls as (1 − λ_{r_k})^T, for any target. Basri et al. (2019), [LIT-612](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-612.md): on uniform spherical data the Gram matrix is a convolution, so its eigenvectors are harmonics, with closed-form eigenvalues per frequency. Active for the kernel regime on uniform spherical data, where every step is proved. It says nothing about networks whose kernel moves. | Active |
| [THEORY-087](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-087.md) v2 | The Bayesian complexity penalty grows as (d/2) log n in a regular model, where the curvature at the optimum sets the Occam factor, and as λ log n in a singular one, where λ is the real log canonical threshold and falls below d/2 when the prior is positive on the optimal set | MacKay (1992), [LIT-623](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-623.md), writes the evidence as best-fit likelihood times an Occam factor, the ratio of posterior to prior accessible volume, which under a Gaussian approximation is P(w_MP)(2π)^{k/2} det^{-1/2}A. When the likelihood dominates, det A grows as n^d, so the penalty is (d/2) log n. Watanabe's WBIC paper, [LIT-616](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-616.md), recovers that case (Lemma 3, Theorem 5) and states what replaces it when the Fisher information is degenerate at the optimum: λ log n − (m − 1) log log n, with λ the RLCT (Theorem 2). The regular half is derived. The singular half is a theorem the record holds only as cited, so this is Proposed. The volume reading of λ is in Watanabe's book, which is unread. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-092](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-092.md) v2 | Behavioural capacity does not fix intelligence: a system with the capacity to respond sensibly to every possible input can lack it, so whether behaviour is intelligent, or the mark of any mental property, depends partly on how it is produced | Block (1981), [LIT-642](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-642.md): the strongest behaviourist conception of intelligence, a capacity to give sensible responses to any sequence of inputs, "whatever they may be", is met by a machine that stores every sensible conversation of a test's length and looks up its next reply, yet "the machine has the intelligence of a toaster". So psychologism is true: two systems alike in all actual and counterfactual behaviour can differ in intelligence through the processing that mediates it. Block (1995), [LIT-630](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-630.md), n. 1: the same machine refutes the wider claim that there is no mental difference without a behavioural one. It is a claim about constitution, not evidence: performance stays evidence for competence. It names no required kind of processing, and its machine is a lookup table, not a trained network. | Proposed |

| [THEORY-105](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-105.md) | Fine-tuning from one pretrained model lands near the edge of a task-specific low-loss region that contains the convex hull of the fine-tuned models, and averaging them moves inward | Gueta et al. (2023), [LIT-658](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-658.md): RoBERTa-base models fine-tuned on the same dataset, the same task family, or any of 12 GLUE and SuperGLUE datasets cluster in weight space. Sampled points in the convex hull of each group beat the group's own members in 88% to 96.7% of comparisons. Extrapolating past the members raises the loss quickly, so the members sit near the region's edge and averaging moves inward. The paper calls the region convex, but shows only that the hull lies inside it, by a probe-based loss. Its reading of model soups and SWA as picking points inside the region is argued in its §8, not tested. Moving from the centroid towards the origin stays low-loss far past the members, which the authors cannot explain. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-106](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-106.md) | In random-features ridge regression the double-descent peak is a divergence of the test error at the interpolation threshold 2N = n as the ridge goes to zero, which a positive ridge keeps finite and a ridge of the tuned size removes; minimum-norm linear regression has the same peak at n = d in exact finite-sample form | Liao, Couillet & Mahoney (2020), [LIT-679](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-679.md): for random Fourier features with n, p and N large together, the test MSE has a closed form through a deterministic equivalent of the resolvent. | [THEORY-107](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-107.md) | Merging models fine-tuned from one pretrained start loses accuracy through interference in parameter coordinates: redundant small updates dilute the influential ones, and influential updates of different models conflict in sign | Yadav et al. | [THEORY-108](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-108.md) | Across load and temperature, the connectivity and output similarity of independently trained solutions predict test accuracy where endpoint curvature does not: a flat but poorly connected landscape generalizes worse than a connected one of the same curvature | Yang, Hodgkinson, Theisen, Zou, Gonzalez, Ramchandran & Mahoney (2021), [LIT-663](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-663.md): thousands of trained networks on a load by temperature grid, measured by the endpoint Hessian, by mode connectivity on a trained Bezier curve between two independent runs, and by CKA of their outputs. | [THEORY-109](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-109.md) v2 | The solutions SGD finds in a deep network lie in one connected low-loss set, joined by simple curves and spanning volumes of measurable dimension, and this is a property of the solutions training finds, not of every minimum | Garipov et al. | [THEORY-111](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-111.md) v2 | Along a low-loss linear path between two networks, every layer's features are the interpolation of the endpoints' features, so averaging weights within a basin averages features | Zhou et al. (2023), [LIT-674](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-674.md): whenever two image classifiers are linearly mode connected, by spawning or by permutation, the features of nearly every layer of the interpolated network are proportional to the interpolation of the endpoints' features. This is layerwise linear feature connectivity, and two conditions, weak additivity of ReLU and a commutativity of weights with features, imply it exactly. Lubana et al.'s Lemma 2, [LIT-669](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-669.md), gives the exact one-hidden-layer case: linear connectivity between interpolating minima forces shared activation patterns, and with shared patterns the hidden features are linear along the path. Measured on pairs at three interpolation points, image classification only. The step to many-model averages such as soups and SWA is not measured. | Proposed |

| [THEORY-113](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-113.md) | Merging models trained on different tasks from different initialisations fails where their features have no counterpart in the other model, and such features grow more common with depth | Stoica et al. (2023), [LIT-665](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-665.md), merge ResNets trained from different initialisations on disjoint label sets. Permute-then-average fails, which they explain by the permuted model lying in a basin for its own task only. Mean cross-model feature correlation falls with depth (0.50, 0.37, 0.27 at three depths). (2020), [LIT-651](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-651.md): from a task-1 solution, a model trained on tasks 1 and 2 together stays on a low task-1 loss line from the start, and one trained on task 2 alone does not. | [THEORY-116](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-116.md) | A linear barrier between two minima that survives the removal of symmetries marks a difference in the input attributes the two models rely on: they compute by different mechanisms | Lubana et al. (2022), [LIT-669](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-669.md): models that rely on a synthetic cue and models that ignore it are separated by a linear barrier even after permutation matching. Fine-tuned models that keep a linear path to their parent keep its cue, and those that lose the path lose the cue. Their Conjecture 1 states this claim's direction. What their Appendix F.3 proves, for a one-hidden-layer ReLU network with interpolating minima, is the converse: linear connectivity forces identical activation patterns, so models relying on attributes of different complexity cannot be linearly connected under any permutation. Zhou et al. (2023), [LIT-674](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-674.md), support that converse in deep image classifiers, where linearly connected pairs have features that blend layer by layer. The stated direction rests on experiments with synthetic cues and on a one-layer sufficiency argument. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-117](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-117.md) | Compositional generalization comes from diversity of combinations, not data volume: in vision models trained from scratch on two-concept grids, unseen pairs are reached as the share of combinations seen grows and not as data of the same combinations grows, and with linearly factored features two seen combinations per value, suitably arranged, determine every unseen one | Uselis, Dittadi & Oh (2025), [LIT-667](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-667.md). In an n × n grid of two concepts with k combinations seen per value, ResNet-50s trained from scratch fit seen pairs and fail on unseen ones; four times the data of the same combinations leaves 60–80% drops, while more values and more combinations help. Features pass from spurious, to decodable but entangled, to linearly factored as coverage grows. Proposition 4.1: under exact linear factorization with a (2n − 1)-dimensional span, k = 2 suffices for a linear classifier to be right on all unseen pairs. Model selection was on the test set, by design, so the results bound what is possible. Synthetic data, two concepts, one from-scratch architecture. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-175](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-175.md) | Cosine similarities to matched anchor points are invariant exactly to the maps that preserve cosines, and independently trained encoders agree in them only approximately: enough for a decoder reading them to transfer untrained between seeds, architectures and languages with loss, while their nearest neighbours mostly differ | Moschella et al. It does not say the maps between trained spaces are isometries, which the source never measures, nor that the transfer needs no paired data: the anchors are paired data. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-180](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-180.md) v2 | In a tied single-head attention layer trained by ridge-penalized empirical risk minimization on high-dimensional Gaussian sequences, weight decay is a nuclear-norm penalty on the query–key map, and the learned map is a soft-thresholded noisy copy of the target: its outliers are recovered target directions and its bulk is finite-sample noise | Boncoraglio, Erba, Troiani, Xu, Krzakala & Zdeborová (2025), [LIT-857](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-857.md): with S = WWᵀ, λ‖W‖²_F is exactly λ‖S‖_* (Appendix A), and in the limit n/d², p/d fixed the trained WᵀW/√(pd) has the law η·ReLU(S0 + δZ − εI), Z ∼ GOE, with δ a noise level that falls with the data and ε a threshold set by λ (Claim 4.1, replica/AMP, checked against Adam at d ≤ 400). It does not say that real transformers' spectra arise this way: the data are isotropic Gaussian, the target is inside the model class, and the agreement with measured spectra is qualitative. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-181](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-181.md) v2 | In a model that decodes the sum of two learned embeddings, at zero training loss with an injective decoder, a training set fixes the generalising representation of addition when its same-answer pairs leave only translation and scale free; for non-modular addition with p = 10 and one-dimensional embeddings, generalisation sets in near the training fraction, about 0.4, at which that becomes likely | Liu et al. (2022), [LIT-858](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-858.md), in a toy built for it: same-answer training pairs force equal embedding sums, equal sums carry answers to unseen pairs, and for addition with p = 10 the fraction at which the forced equations first pin the embedding to a + kb (about 0.4) matches the onset of generalisation and Power et al.'s critical fraction ([LIT-341](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-341.md)). It is shown for one size, 1D embeddings and an operation built into the architecture. It is not shown that larger networks generalise by this mechanism, and for S₃ the networks generalise beyond it. | Active |
| [THEORY-209](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-209.md) | A converged network trained with SGD is not at a point and does not sample its training loss: under a quadratic approximation it samples a Gibbs distribution on a modified loss, isotropic in the Hessian's column space, with probability currents that keep it oscillating, so its speed and spread are set by the learning rate, momentum and batch size | Kunin et al. (2021), [LIT-1011](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1011.md), read in [NOTE-711](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-711.md). Modelled as an underdamped Langevin equation with noise covariance proportional to the Hessian, SGD at the end of training converges to a nonequilibrium stationary state: Gibbs on a modified loss whose curvature undoes the Hessian's anisotropy, with inverse temperature S(1 − β²), in broken detailed balance. A ResNet-18 on ImageNet explores isotropically in a plane where the loss is anisotropic, oscillates at Hessian-dependent rates, and moves at the predicted speed across a hyperparameter sweep. For the learned-structure line, a trained solution is in part a property of the regime that trained it. Proposed: the deep-learning evidence is one network, under assumptions the paper concedes are strained. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-210](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-210.md) v2 | Continuous parameter symmetries stretch a network's minima into connected manifolds along which the loss is flat, and give gradient flow conserved quantities that fix where on such a manifold training ends; finite steps, gradient noise and weight decay break them, so the position along a symmetry orbit is set by initialization and optimizer, not by the loss | Zhao, Walters & Yu (2025), [LIT-970](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-970.md), read in [NOTE-712](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-712.md): a survey, so the dynamical results are secondhand. Continuous parameter-space symmetries (GL, scaling, orthogonal, translation) make minima positive-dimensional and connected, which is one source of mode connectivity. Under gradient flow each gives a conserved quantity, such as layer imbalance, that is fixed by initialization and locates the endpoint on the manifold. Under SGD these are not conserved. Read first-hand (Neural Mechanics; Ziyin et al.), weight decay drives the conserved quantities toward zero, and minibatch noise drives a rescaling symmetry's toward the point where the layers' gradient noise balances. The survey had reported this as imbalance decaying with large learning rates, and a stationary distribution biased toward balanced solutions that a Langevin model does not predict. This is the null-space half that [THEORY-209](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-209.md)'s limiting dynamics leave out. Proposed: one survey, with the SGD results unread here. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-211](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-211.md) v2 | In the stochastic-differential-equation model of SGD, with a gradient-noise covariance that depends on the parameters, minibatch noise drives the difference of squared norms along a rescaling symmetry, at a rate proportional to learning rate over batch size, to the point on the symmetry orbit where the gradient-noise traces of the two parameter groups are equal, whenever both groups carry noise; so at stationarity SGD neither keeps the difference fixed, as gradient flow does, nor lets it diffuse, as isotropic noise does, and differs from gradient descent by a finite amount however small the noise | Ziyin, Li & Ueda ([LIT-1012](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1012.md), read in [NOTE-714](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-714.md)), with the gradient flow conservation law and the Itô term from Neural Mechanics ([LIT-1013](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1013.md)). If ℓ(u, w) = ℓ(λu, w/λ) for every sample, then under the SDE model of SGD d(‖u‖² − ‖w‖²)/dt = −T(uᵀC₁u − wᵀC₂w), with T = η/S. The noise has no component along the symmetry, but its dependence on the parameters produces a deterministic drift through Itô's lemma. The drift points to the noise-balanced point, and weight decay adds to its rate. In a diagonal linear network the stationary distribution follows exactly: it is non-ergodic, has a memory of initialization, and collapses to zero above a critical temperature. The law is re-derived here (2026-10-19) within the SDE model; the tests are small synthetic networks, and whether it holds in deep networks on real data is QUESTION-164. | Active |
| [THEORY-212](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-212.md) | In a two-layer linear network trained by gradient flow, the relative scale of the two layers, which gradient flow conserves, sets the learning regime: balanced layers learn in sigmoidal stages and both build task-specific representations, while strongly unbalanced layers learn exponentially with a static kernel and leave the larger layer task-agnostic | Dominé et al. (2025), [LIT-943](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-943.md), read in [NOTE-715](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-715.md). With whitened inputs and a λ-balanced start, W₂ᵀW₂ − W₁W₁ᵀ = λI, the full gradient flow is solved exactly. λ is conserved and sets the regime. As λ → 0, singular values are learned in sigmoidal stages, as in Saxe et al., and both layers become task-specific. As \|λ\| → ∞, learning is exponential, the NTK is static, and the larger layer stays near the identity while the smaller carries the task at scale ∝ 1/\|λ\|. The paper analyses gradient flow only. Under SGD the conserved quantity drifts ([THEORY-211](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-211.md)), which [QUESTION-081](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-081.md) takes up. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-213](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-213.md) | Every mirror symmetry of a network's loss makes its symmetric subspace absorbing for gradient-based training, and weight decay above a threshold or strong gradient noise makes that subspace favoured, so rescaling symmetry yields sparsity, rotation symmetry low rank, and permutation symmetry merged, identical neurons | Ziyin (2024), [LIT-1014](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1014.md), read in [NOTE-716](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-716.md). If a per-sample loss is invariant under the reflection I − 2OOᵀ, then Oᵀθ = 0 is a stationary condition for GD and SGD. The Hessian is block diagonal there. Above a critical weight decay all minima satisfy the constraint. Under SGD with strong noise the subspace is attractive even at a strict saddle, by a Lyapunov-exponent argument. Rescaling, rotation and permutation symmetries imply mirrors, so they yield sparsity, low rank and merged neurons, with collapse and loss of plasticity as consequences. Proposed: the SGD half is approximate and the network evidence is limited. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-246](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-246.md) | Training objectives that tighten the class clusters of a classifier's last layers buy accuracy on the trained classes and pay for it in new tasks: among ImageNet-trained ResNet-50s, fixed penultimate features with more class separation transfer worse to datasets with other classes, the difference lies in the last few blocks, and fine-tuning removes it | Kornblith, Chen, Lee & Norouzi (2021), [LIT-1044](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1044.md), read in [NOTE-762](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-762.md). Across nine objectives for ResNet-50 on ImageNet, penultimate class separation R² runs from 0.349 (softmax) to 0.845 (squared error), Papyan's Tr(Σ_W Σ_B†)/C from 21.2 to 0.33, and mean linear transfer to eight new-class datasets falls with R² (Spearman ρ = −0.93), from 75.9% to 48.3%. Cosine-softmax temperature raises R² from 0.24 to 0.77 and lowers transfer from 76.0% to 58.9%. CKA puts the differences in the last third of the network; fine-tuning erases them. The cost is for new classes: relearning the training classes, more separation helps. Networks early-stopped near 92% training accuracy; one dataset; correlational across losses. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-331](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-331.md) | Counting the inference a model will serve as well as its training, the least-compute way to reach a fixed quality shifts toward up-front compute as expected inference volume grows: a smaller model trained on more data in Sardana et al., a larger pretrained model over test-time search in Snell et al.; test-time compute won only at low volume and on questions the small model already sometimes solved | Sardana et al. (2024; arXiv 2023), [LIT-1070](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1070.md), read in [NOTE-881](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-881.md), and Snell et al. (2024), [LIT-1063](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1063.md), read in [NOTE-869](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-869.md). Sardana et al. minimise training plus lifetime inference FLOPs at a fixed loss under a Chinchilla-fitted law: the optimum moves to smaller models trained longer as known demand grows (28% fewer FLOPs at 30B quality and 10^13 inference tokens), and 47 runs show loss still falling at extreme ratios but more slowly than the law predicts. Snell et al. match FLOPs between a small model with test-time search or revision and a ~14× larger model on MATH: test-time compute wins at a low ratio of inference to pretraining tokens on easier questions and loses at a high ratio, and on the hardest at every ratio. Both take expected use as a known aggregate; neither has staleness or uncertainty about demand, and Snell's evidence is one model family on 500 questions. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-342](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-342.md) | In AlphaZero on 9×9 Hex, at fixed playing strength, training compute and tree-search compute substitute along a straight line in log–log space, about 15× less search for each 10× more training over about two decades of training compute, down to a one-node search; the trade is measured for one search and counts no games played | Jones (2021), [LIT-1069](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1069.md), read in [NOTE-884](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-884.md). Across about 200 AlphaZero models on Hex boards 3×3 to 9×9, the best Elo for a given training compute follows one change-point curve, shifted by a fixed factor of compute per board row. On 9×9 only, iso-Elo contours of training against test-time search compute are straight in log–log space (fit: log test = −1.2·log train + 0.004·Elo + 29) over roughly 1e14–1e16 FLOPS-seconds of training, ending at a one-node search. One game, one nonstandard implementation, no uncertainty on the fitted coefficients, and no count of how many searches the trained agent will run, so it gives an exchange rate, not an amortization. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-421](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-421.md) | In hyperbolic graph embeddings trained on link-prediction or classification losses, distance from the origin is only a partial reading of hierarchical level: on synthetic trees the root is not innermost and level order is recovered for 69–75% of node pairs, and a loss built on pairwise distances leaves the origin arbitrary | Yang, Zhou, Ying, Chen & King (2023), [LIT-871](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-871.md), read in [NOTE-669](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-669.md). On two synthetic 3-ary trees of eight levels, HGCN leaves the root at hyperbolic distance 1.8–3.3 from the origin where the minimum is 1.2–2.4, the distances are roughly normal rather than leaf-heavy, and radius orders true levels for 69–75% of 5,000 random pairs. Recentring on the centroid plus an outward push raises that to 75–84%. The diagnosis rests on one architecture, two synthetic trees and one table without variance, and the paper does not separate a real failure to order levels from the origin's arbitrariness under losses that see only pairwise distances. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-425](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-425.md) | A connecting path trained only on clean data keeps only the behaviour the clean data ask for: between two backdoored or error-injected image classifiers, models near the ends of such a path keep most clean accuracy and lose the attack, and a path flat in ordinary loss can carry a barrier in adversarial loss that tracks the input Hessian's top eigenvalue | Zhao, Chen, Das, Ramamurthy & Lin (2020), [LIT-668](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-668.md), read in [NOTE-530](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-530.md). A quadratic Bezier path trained on 50–2,500 clean samples between two backdoored VGG-16s on CIFAR-10 has, at t = 0.1, 88% clean accuracy and 1.1% backdoor success with 2,500 samples, and 63% and 2.5% with 50; injected weight errors fail at every point of such paths. Paths trained with the standard loss between regular and adversarially trained models are flat in standard loss with a PGD-loss barrier correlated with the input Hessian's top eigenvalue (0.71–0.88). The proposition offered for that correlation rests on an assumption that would remove the barrier. | Active |
| [THEORY-481](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-481.md) v2 | A linear-attention layer trained on in-context regression learns as a two-layer linear network does: when tasks share the input covariance's eigenbasis and the weights stay aligned with it, then in the long-context limit each input mode is learned on its own logistic curve whose timescale falls with the square of its variance, so learning is staged by the input spectrum, and the layer converges to a preconditioned estimator; at finite context length the modes decouple exactly only when inputs are isotropic, and otherwise couple at order 1/N | Mainali & Teixeira (2025), [LIT-859](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-859.md), read in [NOTE-658](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-658.md). The prediction of one linear-attention layer reduces to p₂ W Σ̂_x q₁ x_q, a product of two learned factors, so averaged gradient flow decouples into modes with τ_α dp_α/dt = q_α(1 − p_α q_α s^∞_α) and τ_α = (ηP s_α²)⁻¹, logistic from a balanced start. The fixed point ŷ = W Σ̂_x [((N+1)/N)Σ_x + (Tr Σ_x/N)I]⁻¹ x_q is the one Ahn et al. and Zhang, Frei & Bartlett found; the trajectory is new. The decoupling into independent modes is exact as N → ∞. At finite N it holds only for isotropic inputs with equal modes: the paper commutes the non-diagonal empirical covariance at (A71) and (A73), and the correct Wishart moment couples the modes at order 1/N. Alignment of the weights with the data's eigenbasis is assumed throughout, the null blocks vanish only in expectation over tasks, and the transfer to non-linear transformers is timing coincidences. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-496](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-496.md) | In few-shot classification and multiple choice by language models up to 175B parameters, whether each demonstration's label is correct contributes little to the gain over zero-shot, while the distribution of the inputs, the label space and the paired format carry most of it | Min et al. (2022), [LIT-814](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-814.md), read in [NOTE-607](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-607.md). With k = 16 demonstrations, labels drawn at random from the correct label set cost 0–5 points against gold labels (2.6 on classification, 1.7 on multiple choice on average) across twelve model–inference combinations and 26 datasets. Out-of-distribution inputs, random English words as labels, or breaking the input–label pairing each cost far more. The random labels always come from the right label set, gaps reach about 14 points on single datasets, and the authors' reading that the models learn no new correspondence at test time is untested on tasks pretraining cannot have taught. | Active |
| [THEORY-504](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-504.md) | In the Gemma Scope sparse autoencoders on Gemma 2, the two fidelity measures disagree by site: residual-stream autoencoders cost more next-token loss than MLP or attention ones at comparable fraction of variance unexplained, and base-model autoencoders transfer to the instruction-tuned model by loss more than by variance explained | Lieberum et al. (2024), [LIT-611](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-611.md), read in [NOTE-482](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-482.md). Across every layer and sublayer of Gemma 2 2B and 9B, JumpReLU autoencoders on the residual stream raise the language model's loss more, when spliced in, than MLP and attention autoencoders whose FVU is about the same; and autoencoders trained on the base model lose little loss on instruction-tuned rollouts while showing a larger FVU gap. The authors' explanations (the residual stream is the bottleneck; fine-tuning re-weights old features) are conjectures, and the authors say no agreed metric of autoencoder quality exists. | Active |
| [THEORY-509](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-509.md) | Under genericity conditions, two dense or top-k (k ≥ 2) mixture-of-experts layers compute the same function only if they differ by a permutation of the experts with their gates and a common translation of the gate weights, and the translation leaves every interpolation barrier unchanged, so expert order is the only gate symmetry alignment must undo | Tran, Trinh, Bui & Nguyen (2025), [LIT-670](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-670.md), read in [NOTE-513](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-513.md). Softmax is invariant to a common shift of scores and the sum to the order of terms, so G(n) = ℝ^d × ℝ × S_n preserves the layer; Theorems 4.1–4.2 show that generically it is all of the gate's symmetry, for dense gating and for top-k with k ≥ 2 (top-1 has an extra scaling). Aligning expert order and then each expert's hidden units gives barriers of 0.0044–0.0066 between GPT-2 MoE layers fine-tuned from different seeds, against 0.14–0.86 without the order step. Every experiment shares and freezes the backbone around the inserted layer, so it is not evidence about independently trained MoE models. | Active |
| [THEORY-510](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-510.md) | How much of an ImageNet image a crop must keep for its label to survive varies widely by class, with architectures agreeing on which classes are fragile, and strengthening random crop raises mean accuracy while some classes lose 20 points or more; how many classes lose is not established | Balestriero, Bottou & LeCun (2022), [LIT-234](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-234.md), read in [NOTE-845](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-845.md). Six pretrained models on cropped test images keep some classes recognisable at an 8% crop and lose others below about 50%, and agree on which. Over 20 ResNet-50 runs, moving the crop lower bound from 100% to 8% raises mean accuracy from about 70% to 76% while "academic gown" falls from about 62% to 40%. The classes shown are hand-picked; the per-class test rejects for 4.4% of classes at the 5% level, uncorrected for 1,000 tests, which alone is not more than chance; and evaluation-set noise is not counted. Theorem 1 does not reach which classes pay. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-521](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-521.md) | In the thermodynamic limit, with examples and capacity growing together at fixed load, generalization error can jump discontinuously with the load when the entropy of hypotheses just above the best error vanishes faster than the training-error energy grows: a spherical perceptron's error falls smoothly as 1/α, an Ising perceptron's drops to zero at a critical load | Martin & Mahoney (2017), [LIT-672](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-672.md), read in [NOTE-542](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-542.md), restating Seung, Sompolinsky & Tishby (1992) and Haussler, Kearns, Seung & Tishby (1996), which the record does not hold. Generalization is set by maximizing s(ε) − α ln(1/(1 − ε)). For weights on a sphere s(ε) ~ ln ε and ε ~ 1/α; for ±1 weights s(ε) ~ −(π²/2)ε² ln ε, the first-order condition has no solution past a critical load, and the error drops to zero. Uniform bounds that see a class only through its size or VC dimension are smooth and blind to this. That deep networks have such a phase diagram is the authors' conjecture, and their mapping of label noise to load and early stopping to temperature is an analogy. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-557](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-557.md) | Low-loss paths between independently trained solutions are found outside supervised image classifiers: graph neural networks trained from different seeds on one graph are joined by quadratic Bezier curves where the straight line has a barrier, and one pair each of diffusion and contrastive models by chains of low-loss checkpoints | Li et al. (2025), [LIT-676](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-676.md), read in [NOTE-529](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-529.md): GCN node classifiers from different seeds, on 12 real graphs and synthetic CSBM graphs, show linear barriers that a fitted quadratic Bezier curve removes. Yao, Zhang & Tian (2026), [LIT-660](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-660.md), read in [NOTE-534](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-534.md): one pair of DDPMs and one pair of small CLIP models joined by chains of checkpoints whose training loss stays under a threshold, where AutoNEB's paths rise steeply on CLIP. The evidence is plots without barrier numbers in the first, one pair per model and retrained anchors in the second. Zhang & Blei's claim of flat paths between LDA's ELBO maxima ([LIT-677](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-677.md)) reports no results. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-566](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-566.md) v2 | In Ganea et al.'s hyperbolic neural networks, linear maps and nonlinearities are Euclidean ones read through the chart at the origin, so a stack of them without biases is a Euclidean network conjugated by that chart, and the curvature acts only through the bias translations and the distance-based output layer | Ganea, Bécigneul & Hofmann (2018), [LIT-879](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-879.md), read in [NOTE-686](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-686.md), which checked the closed forms numerically. Möbius layers are defined as exp₀ ∘ f ∘ log₀, so any composition of them is exp₀ ∘ (the Euclidean composition) ∘ log₀, as the paper notes; only the Möbius bias, which is parallel transport from the origin followed by the exponential map, and the hyperbolic logistic regression's distances to geodesic hyperplanes are not absorbed by the chart. The structural fact is proved; that the networks' gains, confined to a synthetic task and to separating WordNet subtrees in low-dimensional Poincaré embeddings, come from those two operations is this record's inference. [NOTE-686](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-686.md) filed no THEORY. | Active |
| [THEORY-578](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-578.md) | Between two trained networks that compute nearly the same function, a chain of models minimising the summed Jensen–Shannon divergence between neighbours, a discretised Fisher–Rao geodesic found without labels, can be a low-loss path where the straight line in weights has a barrier | Tan, Long, Zhao & Laine (2023), [LIT-662](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-662.md), read in [NOTE-521](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-521.md). Two ResNet-20s at 4× width with LayerNorm, CIFAR-10, permuted by Git Re-Basin's weight matching: the straight line between them still has a large loss barrier, and a chain of 25 models optimised from it to minimise Σ JSD between neighbours on unlabelled training images keeps train and test loss low. One pair, one figure, no numbers in the text. The hypothesis that every geodesic between SGD solutions is mode-connecting is stated, not tested, and a chain whose neighbours agree in output may be low-loss almost by construction. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-675](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-675.md) | Without a shared stable start, the linear barrier between solutions of one objective depends on the structure of the training data: between GCNs it falls with graph density and feature separability and is highest at middling homophily, and between federated-averaging models it grows with client heterogeneity and falls with width | Li et al. (2025), [LIT-676](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-676.md), read in [NOTE-529](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-529.md): on synthetic CSBM graphs the barrier between GCNs from different seeds falls with density and feature separability and peaks at middling homophily; GCN, GraphSAGE and GAT barriers are similar, an MLP's differ. Zhou, Zhang & Tsang (2023), [LIT-666](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-666.md), read in [NOTE-517](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-517.md): FedAvg global models from one random start under more heterogeneous clients are separated by a larger line barrier, joined by a one-bend chain, and the barrier falls with width. Both readings named this account and held it back. The GNN proofs are missing and its barriers are plots; the federated bound treats heterogeneity as isotropic noise, and its lemma and theorem conditions conflict as written. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-683](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-683.md) | Permuting a fixed set of few-shot examples moves a GPT-family model's classification accuracy between near chance and near the supervised state of the art, at every model size tested; the good orders are specific to the model, the spread survives more examples and calibration, and bad orders mostly fail by predicting one label | Lu et al. (2021, ACL 2022), [LIT-833](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-833.md), read in [NOTE-626](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-626.md). All 24 orders of four balanced SST-2 examples give accuracies from about 50% to above 85%, in GPT-2 and GPT-3 models of eight sizes; Spearman correlations of order accuracy between sizes lie between −0.35 and 0.27 (175B against 2.7B: 0.05). The variance stays high up to 32 examples and after calibration. It is a measurement on causal GPT models and text classification, with the transfer analysis resting on one example set, and the paper finds no property of an order that predicts its effect. | Active |
| [THEORY-718](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-718.md) | In a linear-in-parameters model with Gaussian noise and a Gaussian prior, the evidence is exactly the best-fit likelihood times an Occam factor set by the posterior curvature, and when the design grows linearly with n that factor costs (k/2) log n | MacKay (1992), [LIT-623](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-623.md), Eqs. 5–6 with Eqs. 16 and 19–20, read in [NOTE-471](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-471.md): for y = Φw + noise with Gaussian noise of precision β and the prior w ~ N(0, α⁻¹I) on k weights, the posterior is exactly Gaussian, so the evidence is exactly P(D\|w_MP) times the Occam factor P(w_MP)(2π)^{k/2} det^{-1/2}A, with A = αI + βΦᵀΦ. If ΦᵀΦ/n converges to a positive-definite matrix and w_MP stays bounded, the log Occam factor is −(k/2) log n + O(1). Exact for this model class only. The general regular case and the singular case are [THEORY-087](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-087.md), which is Proposed. | Active |
| [THEORY-736](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-736.md) | Two ε-dropout-stable solutions of a multilayer ReLU net, under a loss convex in the output, are joined by a piecewise-linear path whose loss never exceeds the worse endpoint's by more than ε, and joined pairwise paths compose with no higher barrier than their worst | Kuditipudi et al. (2019), [LIT-671](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-671.md), Theorem 1, read in full in [NOTE-544](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-544.md), with Draxler et al.'s (2018) concatenation bound from [LIT-653](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-653.md). Dropout stability gives every solution a half-width copy with the same loss up to ε. Half the units are then free, so working units can be swapped in and permuted at no cost. That joins any two such solutions. It is a statement about dropout-stable solutions only: whether training produces them is [THEORY-109](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-109.md)'s open question, and Theorem 4 of the same paper builds disconnected global minima. | Active |
| [THEORY-741](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-741.md) | A two-layer ReLU student of width at least kM, fitting an orthonormal teacher of M neurons on the sphere, has for any k global minima a global minimum joined to each by a two-piece linear path of minima; and in a deep linear network of depth L and width above 1 + r(L − 1), any r global minima in general position share a global minimum linearly connected to each | Lin, Li and Wu (2024), [LIT-682](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-682.md), Theorems 6, 11 and 18 with Lemmas 7 and 25, read in [NOTE-535](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-535.md) and re-derived by the promotion audit. Two toy models whose minima can be written down: a two-layer ReLU student of an orthonormal teacher on the sphere at population loss, and a deep linear network fitting y = Qx. Spare width lets every minimum be moved, along segments of minima, to one a common centre can reach. No permutation symmetry is used, and nothing is claimed about trained networks. | Active |
